claim: Gbx2 mutant mice lack thalamo-cortical axons (TCAs) as a consequence of abnormal thalamic development.
source: In order to investigate the role of TCAs in tangential migration and radial dispersion of MGE-derived interneurons, we took advantage of the Gbx2 mutant mouse, which lacks TCAs as a consequence of abnormal thalamic development (Hevner et al., 2002; Wassarman et al., 1997) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work (Hevner et al., 2002; Wassarman et al., 1997) and reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The laminar organization of the Gbx2 mutant cortex was normal at birth.
source: Despite the lack of TCAs, the laminar organization of the Gbx2 mutant cortex was normal at birth, as assessed by immunostaining for several layer-specific markers (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The area specification of prospective visual and somatosensory cortices in newborn Gbx2 mutants was comparable to that of wild type littermates.
source: Likewise, the area specification of prospective visual and somatosensory cortices in newborn Gbx2 mutants was comparable to that of wild type littermates (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: The neocortex of newborn Gbx2 knock-out mice showed reduced numbers of GABAergic interneurons in the upper layers of the cortical plate compared to wild type littermates.
source: Across all three primary cortices examined (i.e. prospective M1, S1 and V1), the neocortex of newborn Gbx2 knock-out mice showed reduced numbers of GABAergic interneurons in the upper layers of the cortical plate compared to wild type littermates (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1A and B.

claim: The number of GABAergic interneurons in the middle sector was comparable in mutant and wild type cortices.
source: The number of GABAergic interneurons in the middle sector was comparable in mutant and wild type cortices (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: More than twice as many GABAergic interneurons were found in the lower cortical sector of Gbx2 knock-out mice compared to wild type controls.
source: On the other hand, more than twice as many GABAergic interneurons were found in the lower cortical sector of Gbx2 knock-out mice compared to wild type controls (Figure 1A and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1A and D.

claim: The combined counts of GABAergic interneurons across all cortical layers were not significantly different between wild type and Gbx2 knock-out mice.
source: Despite the differences between upper and lower layers, the combined counts of GABAergic interneurons across all cortical layers were not significantly different between wild type and Gbx2 knock-out mice (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: MGE-derived GABAergic interneurons can reach the neocortex in normal numbers in the absence of TCAs.
source: This indicated that, despite their abnormal layer distribution, MGE-derived GABAergic interneurons can reach the neocortex in normal numbers in the absence of TCAs.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that total interneuron counts were not different between wild type and Gbx2 knock-out mice.

claim: There was no difference in cell proliferation in the E12.5 MGE of Gbx2 knock-out embryos as assessed by BrdU labeling.
source: In agreement with this, there was no difference in cell proliferation in the E12.5 MGE of Gbx2 knock-out embryos as assessed by BrdU labeling (data not shown).
evidence: The claim is stated as an observation from BrdU labeling experiments.

claim: The total thickness of the cortical plate (from layer I to VI) was not different between the two genotypes at birth.
source: Neither was the total thickness of the cortical plate (from layer I to VI) different between the two genotypes at birth (data not shown).
evidence: The claim is stated as an observation from measurements.

claim: The number of Lhx6-GFP+ cells in superficial (MZ) versus deep (SVZ and IZ) routes was not different between wild type and Gbx2 knock-out embryos.
source: However, the number of Lhx6-GFP+ cells in superficial (MZ) versus deep (SVZ and IZ) routes was not different between wild type and Gbx2 knock-out embryos (Figure 1—figure supplement 5), suggesting a defect in the radial dispersion of deep layer interneurons in the mutant.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: The abnormal accumulation of interneurons in deeper cortical layers of Gbx2 knock-out mice is due to a defect in the radial dispersion of deep layer interneurons.
source: However, the number of Lhx6-GFP+ cells in superficial (MZ) versus deep (SVZ and IZ) routes was not different between wild type and Gbx2 knock-out embryos (Figure 1—figure supplement 5), suggesting a defect in the radial dispersion of deep layer interneurons in the mutant.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that interneurons enter the cortex normally but accumulate in deep layers.

claim: Gbx2 mutant mice showed increased numbers of MGE-derived interneurons in the lower layers of the cortex but fewer in the upper layers when BrdU was injected at E12.5.
source: This was done by injecting pregnant females with BrdU at E12.5 and E14.5, respectively, and subsequently assessing the relative distribution of BrdU•Lhx6-GFP double positive cells in upper and lower cortical layers at E18.5. In both cases, Gbx2 mutant mice showed increased numbers of MGE-derived interneurons in the lower layers of the cortex but fewer in the upper layers (Figure 1—figure supplement 6A), suggesting that both early- and late-born interneurons depend on TCAs to attain their normal laminar distribution.
evidence: The claim is supported by BrdU labeling data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 6A.

claim: Both early- and late-born interneurons depend on TCAs to attain their normal laminar distribution.
source: This was done by injecting pregnant females with BrdU at E12.5 and E14.5, respectively, and subsequently assessing the relative distribution of BrdU•Lhx6-GFP double positive cells in upper and lower cortical layers at E18.5. In both cases, Gbx2 mutant mice showed increased numbers of MGE-derived interneurons in the lower layers of the cortex but fewer in the upper layers (Figure 1—figure supplement 6A), suggesting that both early- and late-born interneurons depend on TCAs to attain their normal laminar distribution.
evidence: The claim is inferred from BrdU labeling experiments at different time points.

claim: The relative proportion of Lhx6-GFP+ cortical interneurons expressing the transcription factor Satb1 was not different in upper and lower cortical layers of Gbx2 knock-out mice compared to wild type controls.
source: We also found that the relative proportion of Lhx6-GFP+ cortical interneurons expressing the transcription factor Satb1, which is required for the survival of subsets of somatostatin- and parvalbumin-expressing cortical interneurons (Close et al., 2012; Denaxa et al., 2012), was not different in upper and lower cortical layers of Gbx2 knock-out mice compared to wild type controls (Figure 1—figure supplement 6B and C), indicating that Satb1+ cells were affected in a similar way as the total Lhx6-GFP+ population in the mutants.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 6B and C.

claim: Satb1+ cells were affected in a similar way as the total Lhx6-GFP+ population in the Gbx2 mutants.
source: We also found that the relative proportion of Lhx6-GFP+ cortical interneurons expressing the transcription factor Satb1, which is required for the survival of subsets of somatostatin- and parvalbumin-expressing cortical interneurons (Close et al., 2012; Denaxa et al., 2012), was not different in upper and lower cortical layers of Gbx2 knock-out mice compared to wild type controls (Figure 1—figure supplement 6B and C), indicating that Satb1+ cells were affected in a similar way as the total Lhx6-GFP+ population in the mutants.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that Satb1+ cell distribution was similar to total Lhx6-GFP+ cells.

claim: The lack of TCAs in the Gbx2 mutant likely affected the laminar distribution of different classes of MGE-derived interneurons to a similar extent.
source: Together, these data suggested that the lack of TCAs in the Gbx2 mutant likely affected the laminar distribution of different classes of MGE-derived interneurons to a similar extent.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that both early- and late-born interneurons and Satb1+ cells were similarly affected.

claim: Olig3-CreERT2;Gbx2fx/fx mice injected with tamoxifen at E10.5 showed a significant reduction in Gbx2 expression in the E12.5 thalamic anlage.
source: Olig3-CreERT2;Gbx2fx/fx mice injected with tamoxifen at E10.5 showed a significant reduction in Gbx2 expression in the E12.5 thalamic anlage, as assessed by in situ hybridization (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Olig3-CreERT2;Gbx2fx/fx mice showed a marked reduction of thalamo-cortical innervation compared to Gbx2fx/fx controls.
source: Using retrograde tracing, we could also verify a marked reduction of thalamo-cortical innervation in these mice compared to Gbx2fx/fx controls (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by retrograde tracing data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: MGE-derived interneurons were partially depleted from the upper cortical layers of Olig3-CreERT2;Gbx2fx/fx conditional mutants, but were present in excess in lower layers.
source: In agreement with our observations in global Gbx2 knock-out mice, MGE-derived interneurons were partially depleted from the upper cortical layers of Olig3-CreERT2;Gbx2fx/fx conditional mutants, but were present in excess in lower layers (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2A–C.

claim: Gbx2 is expressed in a subset of MGE-derived Lhx8-positive cells that give rise to cholinergic interneurons in the striatum, but which do not contribute interneurons to the neocortex.
source: It has previously been reported that Gbx2 is expressed in a subset of MGE-derived Lhx8-positive cells that give rise to cholinergic interneurons in the striatum, but which do not contribute interneurons to the neocortex (Chen et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work (Chen et al., 2010).

claim: Gbx2-expressing cells born during embryonic stages do not contribute neurons to the postnatal neocortex.
source: Using Gbx2-CreERT2;dTom reporter mice, we could also verify that Gbx2-expressing cells born during embryonic stages do not contribute neurons to the postnatal neocortex (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by lineage tracing data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: There were no abnormalities in either the complement or laminar distribution of MGE-derived interneurons in the neocortex of Nkx2.1Cre;Gbx2fx/fx conditional mutant mice.
source: In order to rule out any contribution of Gbx2-expressing MGE cells to the cortical phenotypes observed in Gbx2 knock-out mice, we examined the distribution of Lhx6-expressing interneurons in the neocortex of Nkx2.1Cre;Gbx2fx/fx conditional mutant mice, in which the Gbx2 gene is deleted only in MGE-derived neuronal precursors. We found no abnormalities in either the complement or laminar distribution of MGE-derived interneurons in the neocortex of these mice (Figure 2D,E).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2D,E.

claim: MGE-derived interneurons accumulate abnormally in deep layers of newborn mouse neocortex when this is deprived of thalamic innervation.
source: We conclude from these studies that MGE-derived interneurons accumulate abnormally in deep layers of newborn mouse neocortex when this is deprived of thalamic innervation, suggesting a role for TCAs in the radial dispersion of cortical interneurons.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined results of multiple genetic experiments.

claim: TCAs play a role in the radial dispersion of cortical interneurons.
source: We conclude from these studies that MGE-derived interneurons accumulate abnormally in deep layers of newborn mouse neocortex when this is deprived of thalamic innervation, suggesting a role for TCAs in the radial dispersion of cortical interneurons.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that interneurons accumulate in deep layers when TCAs are absent.

claim: Fewer Lhx6-GFP+ interneurons were oriented radially in the neocortex of Gbx2 knock-out mice compared to wild type controls.
source: We found that fewer Lhx6-GFP+ interneurons were oriented radially in the neocortex of Gbx2 knock-out mice compared to wild type controls (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3B,C.

claim: The proportion of radially oriented interneurons was reduced by over 50% in the lower cortical layers of Gbx2 knock-out mice.
source: This was most pronounced in the lower cortical layers, where the proportion of radially oriented interneurons was reduced by over 50% in the mutant (Figure 3C)
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: In the absence of TCAs, excess GABAergic interneurons in the lower cortical layers remain in a tangential orientation.
source: These data suggested that, in the absence of TCAs, excess GABAergic interneurons in the lower cortical layers remain in a tangential orientation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that fewer interneurons were radially oriented in Gbx2 mutants.

claim: Changes in branching morphology of the leading process have been linked to tangential to radial migration switch in migrating MGE-derived GABAergic interneurons.
source: Changes in branching morphology of the leading process have been linked to tangential to radial migration switch in migrating MGE-derived GABAergic interneurons (Baudoin et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work (Baudoin et al., 2012).

claim: There was significantly elevated frequency of highly branched leading processes in GABAergic interneurons of Gbx2 mutants compared to wild type controls in both upper and lower cortical layers.
source: We found significantly elevated frequency of highly branched leading processes in GABAergic interneurons of the mutants compared to wild type controls in both upper and lower cortical layers (Figure 3D,E).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3D,E.

claim: Highly branched leading process morphology has been previously correlated with an inability to switch migration from a tangential to a radial orientation.
source: This type of morphology has been previously correlated with an inability to switch migration from a tangential to a radial orientation (Baudoin et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work (Baudoin et al., 2012).

claim: KCC2 contributes to the hyperpolarizing influx of chloride ions which underlies the inhibitory function of GABA in the mature CNS.
source: The K+/Cl- cotransporter KCC2 contributes to the hyperpolarizing influx of chloride ions which underlies the inhibitory function of GABA in the mature CNS (Rivera et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work (Rivera et al., 1999).

claim: KCC2 becomes upregulated in cortical interneurons as they mature, stop migrating and adopt their final position in the cortex.
source: KCC2 becomes upregulated in cortical interneurons as they mature, stop migrating and adopt their final position in the cortex.
evidence: The claim is stated as established knowledge about KCC2 expression patterns.

claim: In vitro studies have indicated that upregulation of KCC2 is both necessary and sufficient to reduce interneuron motility.
source: In vitro studies have indicated that upregulation of KCC2 is both necessary and sufficient to reduce interneuron motility (Bortone and Polleux, 2009), leading to the idea that KCC2 may function as a stop signal for migratory GABAergic interneurons once they reach their destination in the neocortex.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work (Bortone and Polleux, 2009).

claim: KCC2 may function as a stop signal for migratory GABAergic interneurons once they reach their destination in the neocortex.
source: In vitro studies have indicated that upregulation of KCC2 is both necessary and sufficient to reduce interneuron motility (Bortone and Polleux, 2009), leading to the idea that KCC2 may function as a stop signal for migratory GABAergic interneurons once they reach their destination in the neocortex.
evidence: The claim is inferred from previous in vitro studies showing KCC2's effect on motility.

claim: At birth, most KCC2-expressing cells were also positive for Lhx6-GFP.
source: At birth, most KCC2-expressing cells were also positive for Lhx6-GFP (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The proportion of GABAergic interneurons expressing KCC2 was significantly elevated in the lower cortical layers of Gbx2 knock-out mice.
source: Interestingly, the proportion of GABAergic interneurons expressing KCC2 was significantly elevated in the lower cortical layers of Gbx2 knock-out mice (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Abnormal upregulation of KCC2 expression may restrict the radial dispersion of interneurons in the Gbx2 mutant.
source: This suggested that abnormal upregulation of KCC2 expression may restrict the radial dispersion of interneurons in the Gbx2 mutant.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation of elevated KCC2 expression in Gbx2 mutants.

claim: Significantly more Lhx6-GFP+ cells were observed in the cortical plate at E16.5 in Kcc2 mutants compared to wild type embryos.
source: In the Kcc2 mutant, we observed significantly more Lhx6-GFP+ cells in the cortical plate at E16.5 compared to wild type embryos (Figure 5A,B), suggesting premature tangential to radial orientation switch and dispersion of GABAergic interneurons in the absence of KCC2.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 5A,B.

claim: Kcc2 mutants show premature tangential to radial orientation switch and dispersion of GABAergic interneurons.
source: In the Kcc2 mutant, we observed significantly more Lhx6-GFP+ cells in the cortical plate at E16.5 compared to wild type embryos (Figure 5A,B), suggesting premature tangential to radial orientation switch and dispersion of GABAergic interneurons in the absence of KCC2.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation of more interneurons in the cortical plate at E16.5 in Kcc2 mutants.

claim: By E18.5, the number of GABAergic interneurons in upper cortical layers was comparable in wild type and Kcc2 mutant embryos.
source: By E18.5, the number of GABAergic interneurons in upper cortical layers was comparable in wild type and mutant embryos (Figure 5A,B) and this was also maintained at birth (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 5A,B.

claim: Deletion of Kcc2 in Gbx2/Kcc2 double mutants rescued the defect in interneuron distribution observed in Gbx2 knock-out mice.
source: As before, Gbx2 knock-out mice presented excess GABAergic interneurons in lower cortical layers, but fewer in upper layers, compared to wild type controls (Figure 5C,D). Interestingly, this defect was rescued upon deletion of Kcc2 in the double mutants (Figure 5C,D), supporting the notion that KCC2 restrains radial dispersion of MGE-derived GABAergic interneurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 5C,D.

claim: KCC2 restrains radial dispersion of MGE-derived GABAergic interneurons.
source: As before, Gbx2 knock-out mice presented excess GABAergic interneurons in lower cortical layers, but fewer in upper layers, compared to wild type controls (Figure 5C,D). Interestingly, this defect was rescued upon deletion of Kcc2 in the double mutants (Figure 5C,D), supporting the notion that KCC2 restrains radial dispersion of MGE-derived GABAergic interneurons.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the rescue of the Gbx2 phenotype by Kcc2 deletion.

claim: Electroporation of shKCC2 normalized the distribution of GABAergic interneurons in Gbx2 mutants, eliminating their differences compared to wild type controls.
source: In contrast, electroporation of shKCC2 normalized the distribution of GABAergic interneurons in the Gbx2 mutants, eliminating their differences compared to wild type controls (Figure 5G); a result that was in agreement with the data obtained in double knock-out embryos.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: TCA-derived signals may be responsible for limiting KCC2 levels in migratory GABAergic interneurons thereby facilitating their tangential to radial orientation switch and cortical invasion.
source: Together, these results suggested the possibility that TCA-derived signals may be responsible for limiting KCC2 levels in migratory GABAergic interneurons thereby facilitating their tangential to radial orientation switch and cortical invasion.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined results of KCC2 deletion experiments.

claim: KCC2 levels can be downregulated by NMDA receptor (NMDAR) activity.
source: KCC2 levels can be downregulated by NMDA receptor (NMDAR) activity (Lee et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work (Lee et al., 2011).

claim: Activation of NMDARs has been shown to induce proteolytic cleavage of KCC2 by the calcium-dependent protease calpain.
source: Activation of NMDARs has been shown to induce proteolytic cleavage of KCC2 by the calcium-dependent protease calpain (Puskarjov et al., 2012; Zhou et al., 2012a).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work (Puskarjov et al., 2012; Zhou et al., 2012a).

claim: Both Vglut1 and Vglut2 genes need to be inactivated to completely abolish glutamate release from TCAs in the adult mouse brain.
source: It has been reported that both Vglut1 (also known as Slc17a6) and Vglut2 genes need to be inactivated to completely abolish glutamate release from TCAs in the adult mouse brain (Li et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work (Li et al., 2013).

claim: In newborn mice, neither thalamic nuclei nor TCAs nor neocortex express detectable levels of VGLUT1.
source: In newborn mice, however, we found that neither thalamic nuclei nor TCAs (as labeled by 5HTT immunostaining) nor neocortex express detectable levels of VGLUT1 (Figure 6A), a result that is in agreement with previous observations (Kaneko and Fujiyama, 2002; Nakamura et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 6A and citations to previous work.

claim: Abundant expression of VGLUT2 was detected in TCAs of the newborn mouse neocortex.
source: In contrast, we detected abundant expression of VGLUT2 in TCAs of the newborn mouse neocortex, which was completely abrogated in cortices of newborn Gbx2 knock-out mice, confirming its TCA origin (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: VGLUT2 expression in TCAs was completely abrogated in cortices of newborn Gbx2 knock-out mice, confirming its TCA origin.
source: In contrast, we detected abundant expression of VGLUT2 in TCAs of the newborn mouse neocortex, which was completely abrogated in cortices of newborn Gbx2 knock-out mice, confirming its TCA origin (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: VGLUT1 expression remained undetectable in TCAs from Olig3-CreERT2;Vglut2Δ/fx conditional mutant mice lacking VGLUT2.
source: Importantly, VGLUT1 expression remained undetectable in TCAs from Olig3-CreERT2;Vglut2Δ/fx conditional mutant mice lacking VGLUT2 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: At birth, wild type (Vglut2+/+) and Vglut2Δ/fx mice showed indistinguishable distribution of GABAergic interneurons in upper and lower layers of the neocortex.
source: At birth, wild type (Vglut2+/+) and Vglut2Δ/fx mice showed indistinguishable distribution of GABAergic interneurons in upper and lower layers of the neocortex (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Olig3-CreERT2;Vglut2Δ/fx conditional mutant mice showed a phenotype similar to that of denervated cortex, namely elevated numbers of GABAergic interneurons in lower cortical layers but reduced in upper layers.
source: In contrast, Olig3-CreERT2;Vglut2Δ/fx conditional mutant mice showed a phenotype similar to that of denervated cortex, namely elevated numbers of GABAergic interneurons in lower cortical layers but reduced in upper layers (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: A greater proportion of GABAergic interneurons expressed KCC2 in conditional mutant mice lacking VGLUT2 in TCAs compared to both wild type and Vglut2Δ/fx controls.
source: In addition, a greater proportion of GABAergic interneurons expressed KCC2 in conditional mutant mice lacking VGLUT2 in TCAs compared to both wild type and Vglut2Δ/fx controls (Figure 6D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Glutamate derived from TCAs restricts the expression of KCC2 in GABAergic interneurons to facilitate their radial dispersion and cortical invasion.
source: Together, these data support the idea that glutamate derived from TCAs restricts the expression of KCC2 in GABAergic interneurons to facilitate their radial dispersion and cortical invasion.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined results of Vglut2 deletion experiments.

claim: At birth, NMDARs in MGE-derived interneurons primarily contain the NR2B subunit, with NR2A expression appearing at later stages.
source: Electrophysiological and expression studies have shown that, at birth, NMDARs in MGE-derived interneurons primarily contain the NR2B subunit (also known as Grin2b), with NR2A expression appearing at later stages (Manent et al., 2006; Matta et al., 2013; Monyer et al., 1994).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work (Manent et al., 2006; Matta et al., 2013; Monyer et al., 1994).

claim: MGE cells that received shNR2B constructs were fewer in upper cortical layers but more abundant in lower layers, similar to the phenotype observed in Gbx2 and Vglut2 mutant mice.
source: Importantly, compared to the sh-control, MGE cells that received either of the two shNR2B constructs, or both combined, were fewer in upper cortical layers but more abundant in lower layers, similar to the phenotype observed in Gbx2 and Vglut2 mutant mice (Figure 7B).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: A higher proportion of KCC2+ cells was found among GABAergic interneurons that had been depleted of NR2B by in utero electroporation compared to control shRNA.
source: We investigated expression of KCC2 in GABAergic interneurons that had been depleted of NR2B by in utero electroporation and found a higher proportion of KCC2+ cells compared to control shRNA (Figure 7C and D), in agreement with negative regulation of KCC2 expression by NMDAR activity.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 7C and D.

claim: NMDAR activity negatively regulates KCC2 expression.
source: We investigated expression of KCC2 in GABAergic interneurons that had been depleted of NR2B by in utero electroporation and found a higher proportion of KCC2+ cells compared to control shRNA (Figure 7C and D), in agreement with negative regulation of KCC2 expression by NMDAR activity.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that NR2B knockdown increased KCC2 expression.

claim: NMDAR activity, and the NR2B subunit in particular, are required for radial dispersion and correct laminar distribution of cortical GABAergic interneurons by restricting the levels of KCC2 in these cells.
source: Together, these results indicated that NMDAR activity, and the NR2B subunit in particular, are required for radial dispersion and correct laminar distribution of cortical GABAergic interneurons by restricting the levels of KCC2 in these cells.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined results of NR2B knockdown experiments.

claim: Calpain is activated by NMDAR-mediated Ca2+ influx and can proteolytically cleave KCC2.
source: Calpain is activated by NMDAR-mediated Ca2+ influx and can proteolytically cleave KCC2 (Puskarjov et al., 2012; Zhou et al., 2012a).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work (Puskarjov et al., 2012; Zhou et al., 2012a).

claim: Treatment with calpain inhibitor MDL28170 resulted in decreased numbers of GABAergic interneurons in upper cortical layers but increased numbers in lower layers.
source: We found that treatment with MDL28170 resulted in decreased numbers of GABAergic interneurons in upper cortical layers but increased numbers in lower layers (Figure 8A,B), mimicking the effects of TCA ablation in Gbx2 mutant mice, loss of thalamic Vglut2 and NR2B knock-down in MGE-derived interneurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 8A,B.

claim: Treatment with MDL28170 elevated the proportion of KCC2-expressing MGE-derived interneurons in neocortex compared to vehicle treatment.
source: Treatment with MDL28170 also elevated the proportion of KCC2-expressing MGE-derived interneurons in neocortex compared to vehicle treatment (Figure 8C).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: MDL28170 had no effect on the laminar distribution of GABAergic interneurons in mice lacking KCC2.
source: Interestingly, MDL28170 had no effect on the laminar distribution of GABAergic interneurons in mice lacking KCC2 (Figure 8D), indicating that the effects of calpain on the radial dispersion of cortical GABAergic interneurons are dependent on KCC2.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: The effects of calpain on the radial dispersion of cortical GABAergic interneurons are dependent on KCC2.
source: Interestingly, MDL28170 had no effect on the laminar distribution of GABAergic interneurons in mice lacking KCC2 (Figure 8D), indicating that the effects of calpain on the radial dispersion of cortical GABAergic interneurons are dependent on KCC2.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that calpain inhibition had no effect in Kcc2 mutants.

claim: Olig3-Cre;Gbx2fx/fx mutants survive postnatally, up to 5–6 weeks after birth.
source: Unlike global Gbx2 knock-out mice, Olig3-Cre;Gbx2fx/fx mutants survive postnatally, up to 5–6 weeks after birth (Vue et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work (Vue et al., 2013).

claim: Deletion of Gbx2 in Olig3-Cre;Gbx2fx/fx mice is restricted to the thalamus and results in severe deficits in TCAs that persist into postnatal stages.
source: Similar to the Olig3-CreERT2;Gbx2fx/fx strain, deletion of Gbx2 in Olig3-Cre;Gbx2fx/fx mice is restricted to the thalamus and results in severe deficits in TCAs that persist into postnatal stages (Vue et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work (Vue et al., 2013).

claim: At birth, Olig3-Cre;Gbx2fx/fx mice displayed lower numbers of MGE-derived Lhx6+ GABAergic interneurons in the upper layers of the cortex but excess in the lower layers.
source: At birth, Olig3-Cre;Gbx2fx/fx mice displayed lower numbers of MGE-derived Lhx6+ GABAergic interneurons in the upper layers of the cortex but excess in the lower layers, in agreement with our observations in the tamoxifen-inducible strain (Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claim: A significant reduction in PV interneurons was detected in layers II/III and IV of V1 cortex in three week old Olig3-Cre;Gbx2fx/fx mutant mice.
source: Importantly, we detected a significant reduction in PV interneurons in layers II/III and IV of V1 cortex in three week old Olig3-Cre;Gbx2fx/fx mutant mice (Figure 9A).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 9A.

claim: Significantly lower numbers of SST interneurons were found in cortical layers II/III of three week old Olig3-Cre;Gbx2fx/fx mutants compared to control littermates.
source: We also found significantly lower numbers of SST interneurons in cortical layers II/III of the mutants compared to control littermates (Figure 9B).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 9B.

claim: The absence of TCAs results in permanent deficits in the normal complement of GABAergic interneurons in the neocortex.
